paragraphs.text: Noonan syndrome-like disorder with loose anagen hair (NSLH; Mazzanti syndrome) is a RASopathy. Its features include Noonan syndrome-like craniofacial features, cardiac defects, cognitive deficits and behavioral problems, and reduced growth that is generally associated with growth hormone (GH) deficiency. Patients also have darkly pigmented skin and a distinctive combination of ectodermal anomalies, including loose anagen hair (Garavelli et al., 2015). Couser et al. (2018) noted that the disorder has the typical features of Noonan syndrome plus macrocephaly and loose anagen hair, and that intellectual disability is more common than in Noonan syndrome. The disorder is virtually always caused by the invariant SHOC2 c.4A-G (p.Ser2Gly) mutation (Capalbo et al., 2012; Garavelli et al., 2015).

They also had a unique combination of ectodermal abnormalities: darkly pigmented, hairless skin and hair defined as loose anagen hair. Two of the 3 children had mild dilatation of the pulmonary root.

paragraphs.text: Cordeddu et al. (2009) found that 25 patients with a SHOC2 mutation shared a consistent phenotype, previously termed Noonan-like syndrome with loose anagen hair. Facial features looked typical of Noonan syndrome. Patients had reduced growth, often with proven GH deficiency, along with cognitive deficits and hyperactive behavior that improved with age. Their hair was easily pluckable, sparse, thin, and slow-growing, and microscopy confirmed loose anagen hair in 12. Most patients had darkly pigmented skin with eczema or ichthyosis. Most also had cardiac anomalies, among which mitral valve dysplasia and septal defects were overrepresented. The voice was hypernasal. As infants, several patients had been thought to have features suggestive of Costello or cardiofaciocutaneous (CFC) syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Komatsuzaki et al. (2010) reported that all 8 of their patients with the SHOC2 S2G mutation had short stature, sparse hair, and atopic skin. Six had severe mental retardation and easily pluckable hair, and 1 had leukocytosis. The authors concluded that the clinical manifestations partially overlap with typical Noonan or CFC syndrome, and that easily pluckable/loose anagen hair is a distinctive feature of SHOC2 mutation-positive patients.

paragraphs.text: Capalbo et al. (2012) described 2 girls with NSLH, each born to nonconsanguineous parents. Patient 1 was born at 34 weeks after a pregnancy complicated by polyhydramnios. She was referred at age 7 years for severe short stature (height -5.7 SDS), and her bone age was delayed by 3 years. She had macrocephaly, high forehead, epicanthic folds, palpebral ptosis, hypertelorism, a high narrow palate, pterygium colli, pectus excavatum with widely spaced nipples, and deep palmar and plantar creases. She had mild psychomotor delay (IQ 52) and a hypoplastic corpus callosum. Over time she developed nail dystrophy, sparse and easily pulled hair, and dark hairless skin. At 9 years of age she developed complex motor and vocal tics, followed by a generalized seizure. MRI also showed a diffuse reduction in white matter.

paragraphs.text: Choi et al. (2015) reported a girl who was diagnosed with NSLH at age 6 years on the basis of profound short stature and ectodermal anomalies, including sparse, easily pluckable hair. At age 10 years she had recurrent left hemiplegia from transient ischemic attacks. Cerebrovascular imaging showed occlusion or narrowing of both internal carotid arteries and both middle cerebral arteries, with distal moyamoya-like vessels. The authors stated that this was the first reported case of NSLH with moyamoya syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Cordeddu et al. (2009) studied 96 patients with Noonan syndrome who had no mutations in the known genes. In 4 unrelated sporadic patients, they identified a heterozygous 4A-G transition in the SHOC2 gene, predicting a ser2-to-gly (S2G) substitution. In a further 410 mutation-negative patients with Noonan syndrome or a related phenotype, they found the same mutation in 21. This gave a total of 25 patients, who shared a phenotype of Noonan-like syndrome with loose anagen hair. The mutation was de novo in all families in which parental DNA was available, and it was present in several tissues, pointing to germline origin. The S2G substitution created an N-myristoylation site, leading to myristoylation of SHOC2 and its constitutive targeting to the plasma membrane. The mutant did not translocate to the nucleus after EGF stimulation, and in Neuro2A cells it enhanced EGF-dependent ERK phosphorylation. In C. elegans, SHOC2 S2G could not replace sur-8 and caused neomorphic vulval morphogenesis defects.
